## What BirdFlow does (plain-language version)

eBird tells us **where** a species is each week, but not **which birds went
where**. It's like having 52 weekly photos of a crowd without knowing how
any one person moved between photos.

BirdFlow (Fuentes et al. 2023) fills that gap. It learns week-to-week
movement probabilities that (a) reproduce eBird's weekly maps and (b) favor
energetically cheaper moves, tuned against real GPS-tracked birds. We can
then **simulate** individual birds: start one somewhere in the species'
distribution at the start of the migration season, step it forward week by week by drawing from those
probabilities, and record the path.

**These are synthetic routes, not tracked birds.** Every figure and the
website must say so. Their value is in the aggregate: 200 simulated birds
show the shape of the migration, but no single line is a real bird.

**Outputs** (`<season>` comes from `SEASON_LABEL` in config.R):

- `data/derived/routes/<species>_<season>_routes.geojson`: one point per bird
  per week (for the animated map)
- `data/derived/routes/<species>_<season>_lines.geojson`: one line per bird
  (for static maps)
- `figures/03_<season>_routes_<species>.png`

```{r setup}
source(here::here("R", "config.R"))

library(BirdFlowR)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

# Only species with a BirdFlow model that covers our season (decided in 01).
route_species <- read_csv(file.path(PATHS$derived, "species_selection.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(selected, use == "routes + abundance")

route_species |> select(species_code, common_name, bf_model)
```

## Study area (same definition as notebook 02)
source(here::here("R", "study_area.R"))

states <- study_states()   # one polygon per state, CONUS Albers (EPSG:5070)

# One merged polygon for the whole flyway study area, plus the focus state.
study_area <- states |> summarise(name = "Pacific Flyway (study states)")
focus_area <- states |> filter(state == FOCUS_STATE) |>
  mutate(name = tools::toTitleCase(FOCUS_STATE)) |> select(name)

areas <- bind_rows(study_area, focus_area)

ggplot(states) + geom_sf() + labs(title = "Study area states") + theme_minimal()

```{r study-area}
# Shared definition from R/study_area.R: one merged polygon, EPSG:5070.
source(here::here("R", "study_area.R"))
study_area <- study_states(merge = TRUE)

# Basemap of North + Central America for context in the figures.
basemap <- maps::map("world", regions = c("USA", "Canada", "Mexico",
                     "Guatemala", "Belize", "Honduras", "El Salvador",
                     "Nicaragua", "Costa Rica", "Panama"),
                     plot = FALSE, fill = TRUE) |>
  st_as_sf()
# Same datum fix as in R/study_area.R: label as WGS84 so plotting never
# depends on downloading PROJ correction grids.
basemap <- suppressWarnings(st_set_crs(basemap, 4326))
```

## Generate routes

```{r route-fn}
#' Simulate migration routes for one species and save them as GeoJSON.
#'
#' Returns the route points (sf) invisibly so we can also plot them here.
simulate_routes <- function(code, model_name) {

  # load_model() downloads the model once and caches it locally. The cache
  # lives outside our repo (BirdFlowR's own folder), like the eBird data.
  bf <- load_model(model_name)

  # Re-set the seed for EACH species, so a species' routes don't change
  # when we add or remove another species from the list.
  set.seed(RANDOM_SEED)

  # route() picks N_ROUTES starting cells by sampling the species'
  # distribution at the start of the season, then walks each simulated bird
  # forward one week at a time until the season ends.
  # SEASON_BIRDFLOW ("spring" or "fall") comes from config.R; BirdFlowR
  # treats them as aliases for pre-/post-breeding migration.
  # season_buffer = 1 (the default) adds one week on each side of eBird's
  # season dates so birds have time to "depart" and "arrive".
  # NOTE: older tutorials use route_migration(); it's deprecated — route()
  # is its replacement.
  rts <- route(bf, n = N_ROUTES, season = SEASON_BIRDFLOW)

  # rts is a list; the table of points lives in rts$data. route() already
  # converted each point to lon/lat (WGS84), which is what web maps need,
  # so we build the sf object straight from those columns.
  pts <- rts$data |>
    st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
    transmute(
      species_code = code,
      route_id,
      date,                       # week of the typical year
      timestep,                   # eBird week number (1–52)
      stay_len                    # weeks spent at this cell (stopovers > 1)
    )

  # One line per simulated bird, drawn through its weekly points in order.
  lines <- pts |>
    arrange(route_id, date) |>
    group_by(species_code, route_id) |>
    summarise(do_union = FALSE, .groups = "drop") |>
    st_cast("LINESTRING")

  # Flag routes that pass through our study area. We keep ALL routes (they
  # show the species' full migration) but the flag lets the website
  # highlight the ones that actually use the Pacific Flyway.
  # The test runs in the study area's projected CRS (EPSG:5070), which is
  # faster and avoids the spherical-geometry issues noted in R/study_area.R.
  lines$crosses_study_area <-
    lengths(st_intersects(st_transform(lines, st_crs(study_area)), study_area)) > 0
  pts <- pts |>
    left_join(st_drop_geometry(lines) |> select(route_id, crosses_study_area),
              by = "route_id")

  # Save as GeoJSON: an open, text-based format that R, QGIS, ArcGIS and
  # web libraries (Leaflet, deck.gl) all read. These are DERIVED products —
  # simulated paths — not raw eBird data, so they may go on the website.
  # delete_dsn = TRUE overwrites the file if we re-run the notebook.
  st_write(pts, file.path(PATHS$routes, paste0(code, "_", SEASON_LABEL, "_routes.geojson")),
           delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
  st_write(lines, file.path(PATHS$routes, paste0(code, "_", SEASON_LABEL, "_lines.geojson")),
           delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)

  invisible(list(points = pts, lines = lines))
}
```

```{r run}
routes <- map2(route_species$species_code, route_species$bf_model,
               simulate_routes) |>
  set_names(route_species$species_code)
```

## Quick checks

How many simulated birds per species pass through the study states? This is
the first rough answer to 'how much does this species use the Pacific
Flyway?' It cross-checks the population shares from notebook 02: a species
with a high share there should have a high fraction of routes here.

```{r check}
map_dfr(routes, \(r) st_drop_geometry(r$lines)) |>
  group_by(species_code) |>
  summarise(routes = n(),
            through_study_area = sum(crosses_study_area),
            pct = scales::percent(mean(crosses_study_area)))
```

## Static maps

```{r maps, fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
plot_routes <- function(code) {
  name <- route_species$common_name[route_species$species_code == code]
  lines <- routes[[code]]$lines

  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = basemap, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
    geom_sf(data = study_area, fill = NA, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.4) +
    # Routes that miss the study area: faint, for context.
    geom_sf(data = filter(lines, !crosses_study_area),
            colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.3) +
    # Routes through the Pacific Flyway: the story.
    geom_sf(data = filter(lines, crosses_study_area),
            colour = "#1f6fb2", alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.4) +
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-140, -75), ylim = c(5, 65)) +
    labs(
      title = paste(name, "— simulated", SEASON_LABEL, "routes"),
      subtitle = paste(N_ROUTES, "synthetic birds from a BirdFlow model;",
                       "blue = passes through the study states"),
      caption = FIGURE_CAPTION
    ) +
    theme_void(base_size = 11)

  ggsave(file.path(PATHS$figures, paste0("03_", SEASON_LABEL, "_routes_", code, ".png")),
         p, width = 7, height = 7, dpi = 200)
  p
}

walk(route_species$species_code, \(code) print(plot_routes(code)))
```

## Limitations to carry into the report

- Routes are **model estimates**. BirdFlow's accuracy varies by species;
  the BirdFlow team publishes validation reports for each model in the
  collection, so cite the one for each species we use.
- BirdFlow cells are coarse (on the order of 100+ km), so routes show
  broad corridors, not exact paths.
- Routes inherit eBird's biases: areas with few birders (much of Mexico and
  Central America) have less certain abundance, so routes there are less
  certain too.
